title: A flame-speed bell and an extinction line both measure how fast chemistry can keep up with transport
summary: The flame-speed figure plots laminar burning velocity against equivalence ratio, one panel per diluent; the extinction figure plots the strain rate at which a counterflow flame goes out. Both are model outputs for the same hydrogen mechanism, and both are controlled by the ratio of reaction rate to diffusion.

media.alt: Three panels titled Ar, He and N2 with 50 percent dilution. Each panel plots laminar flame speed in centimetres per second against equivalence ratio from 0.3 to 6, for pressures 0.1, 1 and 10 atmospheres. Each curve rises steeply to a peak near an equivalence ratio of 1 to 1.5 and then decays towards zero at rich conditions. The helium panel peaks highest, about 530 centimetres per second at 10 atmospheres.

source.caption: Laminar flame speed validation
source.note: Group explainer. Both are simulations with the bundled hydrogen mechanism file (Cantera h2o2_he.yaml, as the flame-speed title says); the flame-speed caption calls it validation but no measured points are plotted.
group: 05_06_extinction_strain: Extinction strain rate, twin premixed counterflow flame, Ar, He and N2 dilution

read_the_figure.question: How fast does the modelled flame propagate, and how strong a strain can it survive, as the mixture, pressure and diluent change?
read_the_figure.axes: Flame speed: x equivalence ratio phi from 0.3 to 6; y laminar flame speed S_L in cm/s, linear, 0 to about 550; panels Ar, He and N2 at 50 percent dilution; curves are 0.1 atm (blue), 1 atm (orange) and 10 atm (green). Extinction: x phi on the same range; y extinction strain rate in 1/s on a log scale from 10 to 1e4; curves are 0.1 atm (blue) and 10 atm (green).
look_at: The bell shape: each flame-speed curve rises from lean conditions, peaks near phi of 1 to 1.5, then falls on the rich side. Hydrogen's peak lies on the rich side of stoichiometric because it diffuses fast.
Compare the panels: He is fastest (peak about 530 cm/s at 10 atm), then Ar (about 370), then N2 (about 300 at 1 atm). The diluent changes the thermal diffusivity and heat capacity.

Compare pressures in one panel: the 1 and 10 atm curves nearly coincide near the peak in Ar, the 10 atm curve is higher in He and lower in N2, and 0.1 atm is the lowest near the peak in Ar and He (in N2 the 10 atm curve is lowest).
Extinction: the lines slope down with phi, and 10 atm lies far below 0.1 atm: at high pressure and rich mixtures the flame survives only weak strain. The He panel has only one curve (10 atm).
read_the_figure.proves: That the model gives physically shaped curves with the expected dependence on mixture, pressure and diluent. It is not validation: no measurement is plotted.
if_wrong: Visible kinks or flat shoulders (for example near phi of 1.5 and 3) are usually a coarse phi grid joined by interpolation, not physics.
Extinction curves that are perfectly straight on a log axis are two computed points joined by a line; the true curve between them may bend.
A missing curve (He at 0.1 atm) means the calculation did not converge or was not run.
must_check: Computed points are marked on the curves: they are not.
Measured data are overlaid when the word validation is used: none are.
The diluent fraction, pressure and initial temperature are stated: the unburned temperature is not on either figure.
Panels share axes so diluents can be compared: yes, flame speed shares y, extinction shares both.
as_drawn: Peak flame speeds read by eye (phi near 1): Ar about 260 (0.1 atm), 372 (1 atm), 365 (10 atm); He about 343, 499, 529; N2 about 230, 300, 225 cm/s.
Extinction, by eye: Ar 0.1 atm from about 8e3 to about 7e2 1/s between phi 0.3 and 6 (a factor of about 11, one decade); Ar 10 atm from about 2e3 to about 20 (two decades).
Flame-speed curves show flat shoulders at about phi 1 to 1.5 and kinks near phi 3, which suggest a sparse phi grid.

terms.meaning: The speed at which a flat, unstretched, premixed flame moves relative to the unburned gas. A property of the mixture and conditions.
Fuel-to-oxidiser ratio relative to the stoichiometric ratio; 1 is balanced, above 1 is rich.
How fast heat spreads through the gas: conductivity over density and heat capacity. It falls as pressure rises.
The velocity gradient that stretches a flame in a counterflow. High strain thins and cools the flame.
The strain at which a counterflow flame can no longer be sustained.
The share of the mixture that is inert bath gas, here 50 percent of Ar, He or N2.
The exponent describing how the overall reaction rate depends on pressure. It sets how S_L depends on pressure.

remember: Flame speed scales as the square root of thermal diffusivity times reaction rate.
A flame speed that is nearly independent of pressure means an overall reaction order near 2.
Extinction strain rate scales roughly as S_L squared over diffusivity: it tracks the chemistry rate.
Hydrogen peaks on the rich side of stoichiometric because of its high diffusivity.
Kinks and straight segments on model curves are grid artefacts until shown otherwise.

understand.title: Why a bell
understand.text: On the lean side too little fuel limits the heat release; on the rich side the mixture lacks oxidiser. In between the flame is hottest and fastest. For hydrogen the maximum shifts rich because the light fuel diffuses ahead of the flame and enriches the reaction zone.

understand.title: Why diluents differ
understand.text: Helium conducts heat and diffuses species much faster than argon or nitrogen, so the thermal-diffusion factor in the flame speed is larger. Nitrogen has a larger heat capacity than argon and absorbs more heat, lowering the flame temperature and speed.

understand.title: Why high pressure kills the flame under strain
understand.text: At high pressure the reaction zone is thinner (diffusivity falls as 1/P) and radical recombination is faster. A strain that stretches the flame faster than the chemistry can respond makes it go out; the extinction strain falls with pressure at rich conditions, as in the figure.

steps.title: Thermal flame theory
steps.note: A flame of thickness delta propagates at S_L when the diffusion time delta squared over alpha equals the reaction time 1 over omega. Eliminating delta gives the square-root law.

steps.title: Derivation by time scales
steps.note: Setting the residence time in the flame equal to the reaction time gives S_L squared equal to alpha times omega.

steps.title: Pressure scaling
steps.note: With overall order m the rate per unit volume goes as P to the m, and the rate per unit mass-based frequency goes as P to the m minus 1. Order m = 2 means S_L does not depend on pressure.

steps.title: Order from two pressures
steps.note: Reading the 1 and 10 atm peaks gives an effective order near 2 for Ar (365/372), about 2.05 for He, and about 1.75 for N2: computed from values read by eye.

steps.title: Extinction scales with the chemistry
steps.note: A flame is extinguished when the strain rate exceeds the inverse of its chemical time, so the extinction strain rate follows the same rate omega that sets S_L.

steps.title: Log-axis lines are exponentials
steps.note: A straight line on a log axis against a linear phi means exponential decay in phi. Two computed points always make such a line, whatever the true shape.

worked.title: Effective reaction order from flame speed
worked.problem: For helium the peak flame speed is about 499 cm/s at 1 atm and 529 cm/s at 10 atm (read by eye). What effective order m follows?

solution.text: Take the log10 of the ratio of flame speeds over one decade of pressure.
Apply S_L proportional to P to the (m - 2)/2.

worked.answer: m of about 2.05: nearly second order overall, so flame speed is almost independent of pressure.

analyze.q: The N2 flame speed at 10 atm is lower than at 1 atm. Using the pressure scaling step, what does this say about the effective order?
analyze.hint: S_L falls with P when m is below 2.

analyze.q: Why would an extinction curve that is a perfect straight line on a log axis make you suspicious?
analyze.hint: How many computed points define it?

analyze.q: Why is the helium panel's extinction plot missing its 0.1 atm curve, and what would you do to find out?

evaluate.q: The page calls the flame-speed figure validation. What is missing for it to be one?
evaluate.hint: Experimental points with uncertainty on the same axes.

evaluate.q: Which of the two figures is more sensitive to the grid in phi, and how would you check?
evaluate.hint: Refine the grid and see if the shoulders move.

create: Redraw the flame-speed panel with markers at the computed phi values and an experimental dataset with error bars overlaid.
Design a third panel that plots S_L squared over alpha next to the extinction strain, to test the scaling.

checks.q: Why does hydrogen's flame speed peak on the rich side?
checks.answer: Hydrogen diffuses much faster than the oxidiser, so the reaction zone becomes richer than the bulk mixture and the flame is fastest for a bulk mixture that is rich of stoichiometric.

checks.q: A flame speed goes from 200 to 400 cm/s as pressure goes from 1 to 10 atm. What is the effective order?
Why does extinction strain rate fall as the mixture gets richer in these figures?
checks.hint: Flame speed falls on the rich side.
checks.answer: Extinction strain tracks the chemistry rate and S_L squared over diffusivity. Both fall on the rich side, so the flame is easier to extinguish.

checks.q: Do the plotted curves show the model is accurate?
checks.hint: Is anything measured on the plot?
checks.answer: No. Without measured data the curves show only the model's behaviour.

checks.q: How could you verify the grid sensitivity of a flame-speed curve?
checks.answer: Recompute with a finer phi grid and compare: if the kinks or shoulders change position or vanish, they were grid artefacts.
